entities.name: Robert of Hereford
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Robert of Hereford, also known as Robert the Lotharingian, served as Bishop of Hereford from 1079 until his death on July 2, 1095. A highly educated cleric originating from Lotharingia (a region spanning modern France and Germany), he was a pivotal figure in post-Conquest England, bridging Anglo-Saxon administrative traditions with Norman innovations. His detailed observations provide unparalleled insights into the mechanisms of the Domesday Book's compilation, making him an indispensable source for understanding eleventh-century English governance and land tenure. His intellectual contributions extended to mathematics and astronomy, reflecting the broader European intellectual currents introduced to England by the Normans.

Elevated to the bishopric of Hereford by William I in 1079, Robert quickly distinguished himself not only as an ecclesiastical leader but also as a scholar and administrator. He played a direct, active role in the Domesday survey, meticulously documenting the process and offering critical commentary on the methodologies employed by the king's commissioners. His *Epistola ad Walcherum* (Letter to Walcher) and other fragments reveal the detailed inquiries, oath-taking, and systematic record-keeping involved in this monumental undertaking to assess royal revenues and land ownership across England in 1086. Robert's background in Lotharingian scholarship also led him to promote the use of the abacus (specifically, the Gerbertian abacus) in England, significantly advancing computational methods for financial and administrative tasks.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Robert of Hereford's writings provide one of the most vital contemporary accounts of the Domesday Book's creation, significantly shaping our understanding of early Anglo-Norman administration. His introduction of the abacus also had a long-term impact on computational methods in England.
